newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Sunday business - Jan 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Sunday business - Jan 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TIMES
-- GE SEEKS BIG STAKE IN BA'S ENGINEERING ARM

General Electric of America is hoping to buy a large stake in British Airways' engineering arm. The move is part of a push by GE to lift the company's service income and also enhance GE's position in the competition to supply BA with engines when the airline places an order for the superjumbo aircraft early in the next century.
-- HAT-TRICK OF BIDDERS FOR NOTTS FOREST

The battle for Nottingham Forest, the struggling Premiership football club, has intensified with the introduction of a third consortium with a 20 million pounds package being backed by North American investors.
-- CLARKE TO RULE OUT RATE RISE

Kenneth Clarke, the chancellor, is poised to rule out a rise in base rates at his meeting with Eddie George, the Governor of the bank of England on Wednesday. But Treasury officials said the chancellor could still be influenced by this weeks's data.
-- WH SMITH WILL SELL PROPERTY TO CUT DEBT

WH Smith is negotiating the sale of some of its valuable branches in order to raise funds to reduce its borrowings and experiment with new formats. The group hopes to bring in 40-50 million pounds from the dale of a quarter of its freehold properties.
-- MORGAN CHIEFS FACE RISK OF LIFETIME BAN BY IMRO

The Investment Managers' Regulatory Organisation (Imro) is coming to the end of its investigation of the Deutsche Morgan Grenfell asset-management business scandal, and is expected to order that at least six DMG executives have their registrations suspended indefinitely.
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- "COPPERFINGER" BURNS HIS FINGERS

Charlie Vincent, known as 'copperfinger' for making millions trading in the copper market, has lost an estimated 10 million pounds through fund manager Alexander Jones, managing director of Bede and Company. The loss of up to half Mr Vincent's fortune is the latest scandal to shake the fund management industry.
-- WOOLWICH FLOAT HITS EARLY CHAOS

A mailing error has left thousands of Woolwich Building Society members in the dark about their eligibility for free shares when the society floats on the stock market. The problem was caused by the use of two separate mailing lists with thousands of members first receiving confirmation of their eligibility for free shares then a second letter stating they did not qualify.
-- IRISH THREATEN TO BAN BUPA

BUPA, the UK's biggest medical insurer, is on the verge of being banned from doing business in the Republic of Ireland following its sale of insurance polices to the public that breach Ireland's Health Insurance Act. The Irish Health minister has threatened legal action to revoke Bupa's licence unless it withdraws its products.
-- MERRETT SELLS LOSS ADJUSTOR

Stephen Merrett, the former Lloyd's deputy chairman who has agreed to pay compensation to Lloyd's and syndicate Names after huge losses, has severed one of his remaining links with the London insurer, selling Bishop International, the loss adjustor, to two insurance lawyers and the Bishop International management.
-- PILLAR GOES ON SHOPPING SPREE

Pillar Property has made a string of acquisitions worth over 70 million pounds. The deals will confirm the groups grip on the booming retail property sector and bring its exposure to the sector to 240 million pounds including its PillarCaisse joint venture with Canadian pension fund SITQ.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- EMU WILL MISS 1999 DEADLINE

Michel Camdessus, president of the International Monetary Fund, has issued the strongest warning yet that European Monetary Union will miss the 1999 deadline. Speaking at a conference in Germany, the influential French financier suggested that it is better to delay EMU than to rush into a new euro-currency with inherent instability.
-- INVENTOR TAKES DTI TO EUROPEAN COURT

James Dyson, the inventor behind the revolutionary Dyson vacuum cleaner, is taking Board of Trade President Ian Lang to the European Court of Human rights over what he calls the unfair practice of inventors having to pay annual fees to keep the patents they hold on their inventions valid.
-- UNICHEM UNLIKELY TO RAISE BID FOR LLOYDS

Unichem looks unlikely to raise its bid for Lloyds Chemists despite a higher offer from Gehe, its German rival, on Friday. The company is concerned that a higher bid might be counter productive and unjustified. Unichem has until Friday to make a counter offer.
-- CLYDE HOLDS OUT FOR HIGHER PRICE

Clyde Petroleum is expected to reveal improved profits for 1996 next week, exceeding forecasts of 27 million pounds stg. The company is also expected to announce details of its higher level of proven and probable oil reserves in the hope of pushing Gulf Canada to raise its 105p a share bid for the company. Advisers to Gulf Canada have stated that they do not expect Clyde to produce anything that would change Gulf's current offer.
-- GAS FIRM ACQUIRES POISON PILL FOR 1 POUND

Centrica, the sales and trading business that will be demerged from British Gas next month has bought the right to use the British Gas trade marek and flame logo for 1 pound stg. Although under the terms of the demerger, if the company is taken over the right to the name and logo could be forfeited.
OBSERVER
-- SELL-OFF WILL CLOSE BENEFITS OFFICES

Government plans seen by the Observer, to sell off the Department of Social security's property estate to the private sector, could see up to half the country's benefit agency offices shut over the next few years, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
-- HALEWOOD PLANT FACES NEW CRISIS

Ford , the car giant, will this week threaten to close its Halewood plant on Merseyside unless unions agree to new working practices and the loss of over 500 jobs. A meeting between senior executive and the unions is set for Thursday. Ford will build its planned new Escort model at Halewood, securing its future, if he cost-cutting measures are agreed.
-- LADBROKE BOOKS HILTON'S GLOBAL REUNION

Ladbroke, the leisure group, looks set to reunite the Hilton hotels brand after a 30 year split. The agreement to be stuck tomorrow between the British group and the US Hilton Hotels Corporation will connect the groups' reservation and marketing systems for 400 hotels in 49 countries and create cost savings of millions of dollars.
-- SOCIETIES' VALUATIONS RAISE CITY EYEBROWS

The Halifax and Woolwich building societies have admitted that they may have to cut the estimated price their shares will trade at when they reach the stock market in the summer. The high valuations put on the two societies by financial advisers caused a bit of a stir in the City when they were announced last week.
-- WE'RE NOT GOING FOR A BREAK-UP, SAY SEARS BOSSES

Directors of Sears, the troubled retail group, have rejected calls from institutional investors for a further break- up of the company, with one board member claiming that demerging is an overrated game.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- SCOTAM 'TO DROP MUTUAL STATUS'

There is speculation in the City that Scottish Amicable, the life insurer, is considering moves that could lead to a stock market flotation or a merger with a bigger rival. The speculation follows failed merger talks last year between Scottish Amicable and Alliance & Leicester building society.
-- SE CALLED TO ORDER

A Stock Exchange committee chaired by UBS equities chief Hector Sant, will tomorrow start to lay down the details of how the new system for order-driven trading in London will operate. The main item on the agenda is block trading and publication rules for UK stocks, ready for the central order book in the top 100 shares that are due to start the new regime.
-- PROBE ON SHARE DEALS

An enquiry has been launched by the Stock Exchange into potential insider dealing in the shares of insurance broker Fenchurch. The brokers has revealed that it is in merger talks with Lowndes Lambert, with both companies forced into a premature announcement following hectic dealing in Fenchurch's shares.
-- BLUE CIRCLE TO CEMEMT US GROWTH

Blue Circle, the UK's biggest cement producer is to expand into the US with a 300 million pounds acquisition. The company is in talks with a prominent cement company based on the east coast of the US, and industry sources claim that the two sides are close to an agreement.
-- RIVALS IN 'BRITISH TELECON' AD WAR

British Telecom, will be accused of staging a 'Great Phone Robbery' in an aggressive advertising campaign by Bell Cablemedia, a cable rival. Posters and newspaper adverts will claim that BT is charging customers 25 percent more than cable phone rates.
